consumer_world_view.title: India in the World
consumer_world_view.subtitle: A plain-English macro view: what the number is, where India stands, whether the direction is encouraging, and why it matters.

cards.label: Size of the economy
cards.standing: One of the world's largest economies
cards.trend: IMF projects real GDP growth around 6.4% in 2026.
cards.why: A larger, faster-growing economy can support jobs, company earnings and government revenue — but size alone does not tell us how well the average household is doing.
cards.compare: Per-person income remains much lower than the economy's global size would suggest.
cards.source: IMF World Economic Outlook / India country page

cards.label: Income per person
cards.trend: Rising over time as the economy grows, but from a much lower base than advanced economies.
cards.why: This is the better reality check on living standards. A country can be a huge economy because it has many people while average income is still modest.
cards.compare: Use this beside GDP size to avoid confusing national scale with household prosperity.

cards.label: Population
cards.trend: Population is still growing, while fertility has moved down sharply over the long run.
cards.why: A huge working-age population can support consumption and growth, but it also raises the need for jobs, housing, education, healthcare and infrastructure.
cards.compare: Scale gives India one of the world's largest consumer and labour markets.

cards.label: Share of world economy (PPP)
cards.standing: A very large share of global output on a purchasing-power basis
cards.trend: India's weight in the world economy has been rising with faster growth than many large economies.
cards.why: PPP adjusts for local prices. It is useful for understanding India's economic scale and domestic purchasing power, though it is not the same as market-exchange-rate GDP.
cards.compare: Think of this as India's share of the world's real purchasing-power-sized economy.

cards.label: Crude steel production
cards.trend: Up about 10.4% from 2024 in worldsteel's 2025 totals.
cards.why: Steel demand and production connect to construction, autos, machinery and infrastructure. Strong output usually means a deep industrial base — though it is also energy-intensive.
cards.compare: China remains far larger; India is clearly the second-largest producer.

cards.label: Coal production
cards.trend: Near record levels; IEA expects another record around 1.095 billion tonnes in 2026.
cards.why: More domestic coal reduces import dependence and supports reliable power, but heavy coal use also increases pollution and carbon emissions.
cards.compare: China is #1 by a wide margin; India is ahead of Indonesia, the third-largest producer.
cards.source: International Energy Agency, Coal Mid-Year Update 2026

cards.label: Milk production share
cards.trend: India has been the world's largest milk producer for years.
cards.why: Dairy is not just food output; it supports millions of rural households and is an important source of regular cash income.
cards.compare: FAO identifies India ahead of the US, Pakistan, China and Brazil in milk production.

cards.label: Road network
cards.trend: National highways and high-speed corridors have continued to expand.
cards.why: Roads affect freight time, logistics cost, access to markets and mobility. Network size matters, but quality, congestion and travel speed matter too.
cards.compare: India has enormous physical coverage; the next question is how efficiently that network moves people and goods.
cards.source: Government of India, Ministry of Road Transport & Highways / PIB

cards.label: Mobile phone manufacturing
cards.trend: India shifted from being a major importer to a major producer and exporter of mobile phones.
cards.why: This shows whether India is moving beyond services into large-scale electronics manufacturing, exports and supply-chain capability.
cards.compare: The deeper test is not only assembly volume but how much component and design value is created domestically.

cards.label: Renewable power capacity
cards.trend: Capacity has been expanding rapidly as India targets much more non-fossil generation this decade.
cards.why: More renewable capacity can reduce fuel-import exposure and emissions, but grid, storage and transmission investment determine how useful the capacity becomes.
cards.compare: India is also among the global leaders in solar and wind capacity.

consumer_world_view.method_note: Curated structural context for non-experts. Rankings are included only when the cited source or an authoritative table supports them. Observation years differ because structural data is not released on one common schedule.
